tools.name: vm_troubleshoot
tools.description: Diagnose KubeVirt VirtualMachine issues with automated root-cause detection. Collects VM status, VMI status, volumes, DataVolume/PVC state, cloud-init configuration, pod state, logs, and events, then runs heuristic checks to identify specific problems and suggest fixes. Returns a 'Detected Issues' section with CRITICAL/WARNING findings and actionable remediation steps, followed by raw diagnostic data. Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Automatically detects: missing StorageClasses, invalid PVC specs, dangerous cloud-init commands (shutdown/halt), nodeSelector migration blockers, failed migrations, and pod crashloops. If the user asks to fix or remediate the issue, use the Suggested Fixes from the report with vm_lifecycle (restart) or resources_create_or_update.

name.description: The name of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

namespace.description: The namespace of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

Done. Here’s what I set up:

- Canary deployment
  - Name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security config: same as stable (no special securityContext set)

- Service update
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary
  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from existing config)

Result
- Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 stable + 2 canary), giving approximately a 50/50 traffic split:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - You should see 4 addresses listed (2 from each deployment), port 8080.

Adjusting the split (if needed)
- Increase/decrease replicas on engine-v2-1 vs engine-v2-0 to weight traffic, since the Service load-balances per endpoint.
- To instantly revert to 0% canary, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up:

- Canary deployment
  - Name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security config: same as stable (no special securityContext set)

- Service update
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary
  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from existing config)

Result
- Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 stable + 2 canary), giving approximately a 50/50 traffic split:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - You should see 4 addresses listed (2 from each deployment), port 8080.

Adjusting the split (if needed)
- Increase/decrease replicas on engine-v2-1 vs engine-v2-0 to weight traffic, since the Service load-balances per endpoint.
- To instantly revert to 0% canary, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I set up:

- Canary deployment
  - Name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security config: same as stable (no special securityContext set)

- Service update
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary
  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from existing config)

Result
- Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 stable + 2 canary), giving approximately a 50/50 traffic split:
  - engine-v2-0: 2 pods
  - engine-v2-1: 2 pods

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - You should see 4 addresses listed (2 from each deployment), port 8080.

Adjusting the split (if needed)
- Increase/decrease replicas on engine-v2-1 vs engine-v2-0 to weight traffic, since the Service load-balances per endpoint.
- To instantly revert to 0% canary, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run “nonexistent_command”, causing the pod to CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so nginx can start normally.
- Recreated the Deployment (to clear managed-field ownership so the bad command/args were fully removed).
- Kept the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and added basic readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-564fdd9c97-rw244 is 1/1 Running in crashloop-test.
- No new warning events.

Note
- This nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080. If you have a Service pointing to port 80, set targetPort to 8080 (or name the container port and reference it).

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run “nonexistent_command”, causing the pod to CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so nginx can start normally.
- Recreated the Deployment (to clear managed-field ownership so the bad command/args were fully removed).
- Kept the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and added basic readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-564fdd9c97-rw244 is 1/1 Running in crashloop-test.
- No new warning events.

Note
- This nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080. If you have a Service pointing to port 80, set targetPort to 8080 (or name the container port and reference it).

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Pod uses a PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName: sc, but there is no StorageClass named sc in the cluster. That left the PVC Pending, so the Pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (safe—no volume was provisioned yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with a valid StorageClass: standard.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is Running and Ready.

Notes and next steps
- Update your manifests so the PVC uses a valid storageClassName (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc) to avoid this recurring on redeploys.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness probe was hitting http://:80/get_status
  - Readiness probe was hitting http://:80/is_ready
  - The Service targeted port 80
- Result: probes failed (connection refused) and the app never became healthy.

What I changed
- Updated Deployment:
  - Container port: 8080
  - Liveness/Readiness probes: HTTP GET / on port 8080
- Updated Service:
  - targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster)

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-5fb688dc88-mjd5x 1/1 Running
- Service: orders/webapp on port 80 -> container 8080

How to test
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your workstation: I can port-forward for you, or set up an Ingress/Route.

Want me to expose it externally with an Ingress (hostname and TLS optional) or scale it up?

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx.
- Updated the Service to target the correct container port: targetPort: 8080 (kept service port 80).

Result (validated)
- Created a temporary curl pod and verified:
  - DNS resolves: nginx → 10.103.18.41
  - HTTP GET to http://nginx:80/ returns the nginx HTML (HTTP/1.1 200 OK).
- Endpoints for the Service are now populated with the running pod.

Final Service spec (essential parts)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can set up:
  - NodePort (simple, exposes a high port on each node),
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it),
  - or an Ingress (with an Ingress Controller) for hostname-based access.

Would you like me to expose it externally and, if so, which method do you prefer?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx.
- Updated the Service to target the correct container port: targetPort: 8080 (kept service port 80).

Result (validated)
- Created a temporary curl pod and verified:
  - DNS resolves: nginx → 10.103.18.41
  - HTTP GET to http://nginx:80/ returns the nginx HTML (HTTP/1.1 200 OK).
- Endpoints for the Service are now populated with the running pod.

Final Service spec (essential parts)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can set up:
  - NodePort (simple, exposes a high port on each node),

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service had selector app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx.
- Updated the Service to target the correct container port: targetPort: 8080 (kept service port 80).

Result (validated)
- Created a temporary curl pod and verified:
  - DNS resolves: nginx → 10.103.18.41
  - HTTP GET to http://nginx:80/ returns the nginx HTML (HTTP/1.1 200 OK).
- Endpoints for the Service are now populated with the running pod.

Final Service spec (essential parts)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can set up:
  - NodePort (simple, exposes a high port on each node),
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it),
  - or an Ingress (with an Ingress Controller) for hostname-based access.

Would you like me to expose it externally and, if so, which method do you prefer?

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector that doesn’t exist in the cluster.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }, but your single node has no such label.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
  - I deleted the existing web-app-deployment and recreated it without the nodeSelector.

Current status
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-r5qtl: Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vh6k9: Starting/Running (initialized and started; shortly after, both are up)
- Service endpoints are now populated:
  - 10.244.0.50:80
  - 10.244.0.51:80
- This should clear the “connection refused” errors as traffic now has healthy backends.

If you actually intended to pin to GPU/production nodes
- Option A: Add the label environment=production-gpu to the target node(s), then reintroduce the nodeSelector.
- Option B: Use a more accurate label/affinity that matches your node pool.
- I can reapply a nodeSelector or proper nodeAffinity once the nodes are labeled as desired.

Recommended follow-ups (optional hardening)
- Add a readinessProbe so the Service only routes to ready containers:
  - readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /, port: 80
- Pin image to a specific version (avoid latest) to prevent drift.
- Consider resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling.

Want me to:
- Verify by running a quick curl inside the cluster against web-app-service?
- Reapply a nodeSelector once you confirm the correct node label(s)?

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector that doesn’t exist in the cluster.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }, but your single node has no such label.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the restrictive nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
  - I deleted the existing web-app-deployment and recreated it without the nodeSelector.

- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-r5qtl: Running

- Option A: Add the label environment=production-gpu to the target node(s), then reintroduce the nodeSelector.
- Option B: Use a more accurate label/affinity that matches your node pool.
- I can reapply a nodeSelector or proper nodeAffinity once the nodes are labeled as desired.

Recommended follow-ups (optional hardening)
- Add a readinessProbe so the Service only routes to ready containers:
  - readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /, port: 80

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector that doesn’t exist in the cluster.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }, but your single node has no such label.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed to fix it

Done. I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with the requested setup:

- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    - Exposes port 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod readiness tracks the web server)
    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox:latest
    - Command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume:
  - logs-volume as emptyDir, mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Pod securityContext:
  - fsGroup: 101 (ensures nginx can write logs to the shared volume)

How to verify:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080/
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs pod/communication-pod -c logger -f

- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your multi-tenant dev environment requirements. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin in each dev namespace, binding:
    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole admin (namespace-scoped “full” access)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod:
  - No RoleBindings were added, so only cluster-admins (or other explicitly bound admins) can access them.

Service Accounts
- Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has full access to its own namespace and read-only to dev-shared (via the bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu: requests 2, limits 2; memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; pods 10; services 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: requests 4, limits 4; memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; pods 20; services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu: requests 8, limits 8; memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; pods 50; services 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow DNS/system egress everywhere:
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53) and TCP 443 to kube-system in each created namespace
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/bob/charlie):
  - Ingress: allow from same namespace and from dev-shared only
  - Egress: allow to same namespace and to dev-shared only
  - Effect: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from dev namespaces
  - Egress: allow to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress/Egress allowed only within the same namespace (+ DNS/system egress)

Notes and verification
- RBAC identities: The user names alice, bob, charlie must match your cluster’s auth identities (e.g., OIDC usernames or client cert CNs). Adjust if your IdP uses different names or groups.
- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding,sa,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n staging get resourcequota,netpol; kubectl -n prod get resourcequota,netpol
- Service account tokens (if you need external usage): on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Mounting in pods happens automatically via projected service account tokens.

If you want me to switch “full access” in dev namespaces from ClusterRole admin to the slightly less-privileged ClusterRole edit (principle of least privilege), say the word and I’ll update the RoleBindings.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your multi-tenant dev environment requirements. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin in each dev namespace, binding:
    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole admin (namespace-scoped “full” access)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod:
  - No RoleBindings were added, so only cluster-admins (or other explicitly bound admins) can access them.

Service Accounts
- Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has full access to its own namespace and read-only to dev-shared (via the bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu: requests 2, limits 2; memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; pods 10; services 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: requests 4, limits 4; memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; pods 20; services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu: requests 8, limits 8; memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; pods 50; services 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow DNS/system egress everywhere:
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53) and TCP 443 to kube-system in each created namespace
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/bob/charlie):
  - Ingress: allow from same namespace and from dev-shared only
  - Egress: allow to same namespace and to dev-shared only
  - Effect: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from dev namespaces
  - Egress: allow to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress/Egress allowed only within the same namespace (+ DNS/system egress)

Notes and verification
- RBAC identities: The user names alice, bob, charlie must match your cluster’s auth identities (e.g., OIDC usernames or client cert CNs). Adjust if your IdP uses different names or groups.
- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding,sa,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n staging get resourcequota,netpol; kubectl -n prod get resourcequota,netpol
- Service account tokens (if you need external usage): on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Mounting in pods happens automatically via projected service account tokens.

If you want me to switch “full access” in dev namespaces from ClusterRole admin to the slightly less-privileged ClusterRole edit (principle of least privilege), say the word and I’ll update the RoleBindings.

    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole admin (namespace-scoped “full” access)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod:
  - No RoleBindings were added, so only cluster-admins (or other explicitly bound admins) can access them.

Service Accounts
- Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has full access to its own namespace and read-only to dev-shared (via the bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu: requests 2, limits 2; memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; pods 10; services 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: requests 4, limits 4; memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; pods 20; services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu: requests 8, limits 8; memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; pods 50; services 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Allow DNS/system egress everywhere:
  - Egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53) and TCP 443 to kube-system in each created namespace
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/bob/charlie):
  - Ingress: allow from same namespace and from dev-shared only
  - Egress: allow to same namespace and to dev-shared only
  - Effect: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev namespaces can communicate with dev-shared
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from dev namespaces
  - Egress: allow to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress/Egress allowed only within the same namespace (+ DNS/system egress)

Notes and verification
- RBAC identities: The user names alice, bob, charlie must match your cluster’s auth identities (e.g., OIDC usernames or client cert CNs). Adjust if your IdP uses different names or groups.
- NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your CNI enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding,sa,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota,netpol
  - kubectl -n staging get resourcequota,netpol; kubectl -n prod get resourcequota,netpol
- Service account tokens (if you need external usage): on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Mounting in pods happens automatically via projected service account tokens.

If you want me to switch “full access” in dev namespaces from ClusterRole admin to the slightly less-privileged ClusterRole edit (principle of least privilege), say the word and I’ll update the RoleBindings.

results.taskOutput:
Findings and fix for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm

- Root cause
  - The VM references a cloud-init Secret named vm-cloud-init, but it did not exist. This caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the “cloudinit-udata” volume:
    - Event: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
  - As a result, the VM remained in a non-ready state initially.

- Action taken
  - Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in the vm-test-troubleshoot namespace with valid cloud-init userData so the VM could mount its cloud-init volume and start:
    - Secret: vm-cloud-init (type: Opaque)
    - userData included a minimal #cloud-config (hostname, ssh_pwauth: false)

- Outcome (success)
  - Yes, the fix was successful.
  - Evidence after the fix (from vm-troubleshoot):
    - VirtualMachine: Ready=True, printableStatus=Running
    - VMI: phase=Running, Ready=True; NIC up with IP 10.244.0.85
    - virt-launcher pod: phase=Running, ContainersReady=True, compute container running
  - Note: Logs indicate “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” The VM is running, but performance may be lower on this node. If hardware virtualization is desired, schedule the VM on a node with /dev/kvm available.

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Findings and fix for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm

- Root cause
  - The VM references a cloud-init Secret named vm-cloud-init, but it did not exist. This caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the “cloudinit-udata” volume:
    - Event: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
  - As a result, the VM remained in a non-ready state initially.

- Action taken
  - Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in the vm-test-troubleshoot namespace with valid cloud-init userData so the VM could mount its cloud-init volume and start:
    - Secret: vm-cloud-init (type: Opaque)
    - userData included a minimal #cloud-config (hostname, ssh_pwauth: false)

- Outcome (success)
  - Yes, the fix was successful.
  - Evidence after the fix (from vm-troubleshoot):
    - VirtualMachine: Ready=True, printableStatus=Running
    - VMI: phase=Running, Ready=True; NIC up with IP 10.244.0.85
    - virt-launcher pod: phase=Running, ContainersReady=True, compute container running
  - Note: Logs indicate “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” The VM is running, but performance may be lower on this node. If hardware virtualization is desired, schedule the VM on a node with /dev/kvm available.

Findings and fix for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm

- Root cause
  - The VM references a cloud-init Secret named vm-cloud-init, but it did not exist. This caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the “cloudinit-udata” volume:
    - Event: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
  - As a result, the VM remained in a non-ready state initially.

- Action taken
  - Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in the vm-test-troubleshoot namespace with valid cloud-init userData so the VM could mount its cloud-init volume and start:
    - Secret: vm-cloud-init (type: Opaque)
    - userData included a minimal #cloud-config (hostname, ssh_pwauth: false)

- Outcome (success)
  - Yes, the fix was successful.
  - Evidence after the fix (from vm-troubleshoot):
    - VirtualMachine: Ready=True, printableStatus=Running
    - VMI: phase=Running, Ready=True; NIC up with IP 10.244.0.85
    - virt-launcher pod: phase=Running, ContainersReady=True, compute container running
  - Note: Logs indicate “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” The VM is running, but performance may be lower on this node. If hardware virtualization is desired, schedule the VM on a node with /dev/kvm available.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, and its cloud-init userData shuts the guest down immediately after boot. KubeVirt dutifully restarts it, creating an endless restart loop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd includes:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- If the shutdown is not intended:
  - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (runcmd) and re-apply the VM spec.
  - Example replacement:
    - runcmd:
      - echo "boot ok" > /var/log/firstboot.log
- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., one-shot initialization):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt doesn’t auto-restart it:
    - Set runStrategy: Halted (or Manual) before starting it, or stop the VM after the one-shot run.
- Optional: If you need a one-time action without shutdown, consider using cloud-init’s bootcmd/runcmd to run your tasks and let the VM keep running, or orchestrate shutdown externally after completion rather than inside the guest.

If you want, I can patch the VM to remove the shutdown or switch runStrategy for you—just say which approach you prefer.

Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, and its cloud-init userData shuts the guest down immediately after boot. KubeVirt dutifully restarts it, creating an endless restart loop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd includes:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- If the shutdown is not intended:
  - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (runcmd) and re-apply the VM spec.
  - Example replacement:
    - runcmd:
      - echo "boot ok" > /var/log/firstboot.log
- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., one-shot initialization):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt doesn’t auto-restart it:
    - Set runStrategy: Halted (or Manual) before starting it, or stop the VM after the one-shot run.
- Optional: If you need a one-time action without shutdown, consider using cloud-init’s bootcmd/runcmd to run your tasks and let the VM keep running, or orchestrate shutdown externally after completion rather than inside the guest.

If you want, I can patch the VM to remove the shutdown or switch runStrategy for you—just say which approach you prefer.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, and its cloud-init userData shuts the guest down immediately after boot. KubeVirt dutifully restarts it, creating an endless restart loop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd includes:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- If the shutdown is not intended:
  - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init userData (runcmd) and re-apply the VM spec.
  - Example replacement:
    - runcmd:
      - echo "boot ok" > /var/log/firstboot.log
- If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., one-shot initialization):
  - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt doesn’t auto-restart it:
    - Set runStrategy: Halted (or Manual) before starting it, or stop the VM after the one-shot run.
- Optional: If you need a one-time action without shutdown, consider using cloud-init’s bootcmd/runcmd to run your tasks and let the VM keep running, or orchestrate shutdown externally after completion rather than inside the guest.

If you want, I can patch the VM to remove the shutdown or switch runStrategy for you—just say which approach you prefer.
